q: The galvanic cell shown is built from a copper electrode (A) in 1 M Cu<sup>2+</sup> and an aluminum electrode (B) in 1 M Al<sup>3+</sup>. Using the standard reduction potentials in the table, which cell notation describes the cell as it operates spontaneously?
h: Cell notation lists the anode (oxidation) on the left of the double line and the cathode on the right. The half-cell with the lower E° is oxidized.
w: Al3+/Al has the lower E° (−1.66 V), so aluminum (electrode B) is oxidized and is the anode; Cu2+ is reduced at copper (A), the cathode. The anode goes on the left, written reactant | product: Al(s) | Al3+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s). The position of a beaker in the drawing does not decide the order; the electrode reactions do. Each half-cell lists its own metal and its own ion, so Al and Cu2+ never share a half-cell.
x: This puts copper on the anode side. Copper has the higher reduction potential, so Cu²⁺ is reduced, not Cu oxidized.
Within each half-cell the notation goes from reactant to product. At the anode the metal is the reactant, and at the cathode the ion is.
Each half-cell must pair a metal with its own ion. Al and Cu²⁺ are in separate beakers.

q: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolyzed between inert electrodes. The boxes show a tiny region of the melt before and after current passes. How many electrons passed through the circuit to make the change shown, and at which electrode did the Cl<sub>2</sub> form?
h: Count the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions that became Mg atoms. Each one gains two electrons. Then decide where oxidation happens.
w: Two Mg2+ ions (5 → 3) became 2 Mg atoms, each gaining 2 electrons: 4 electrons. At the same time 4 Cl− ions (10 → 6) lost one electron each to form 2 Cl2 molecules, which also accounts for 4 electrons. Cl− → Cl2 is oxidation, which always takes place at the anode: 4 electrons; at the anode. Counting one electron per Mg atom gives 2, and adding the electrons lost and gained double counts them (8).
x: Each Mg²⁺ needs two electrons to become a Mg atom, not one.
Making Cl₂ from Cl⁻ is an oxidation. Reduction (making Mg) is the cathode process.
The electrons lost by Cl⁻ are the same electrons gained by Mg²⁺. Count them once.

q: In a basic solution, chlorate ion is reduced to chloride ion, as shown (unbalanced). Which is the correctly balanced half-reaction for basic solution?
h: Chlorine goes from +5 to −1. In basic solution, balance O with H<sub>2</sub>O and H with OH<sup>−</sup>, then check the charge on both sides.
w: Cl changes from +5 to −1, a gain of 6 electrons. Balancing in acid gives ClO3− + 6 H+ + 6 e− → Cl− + 3 H2O; adding 6 OH− to both sides turns the 6 H+ into 6 H2O and leaves ClO3− + 3 H2O + 6 e− → Cl− + 6 OH− (charge −7 on each side). The H+ version is right only for acid, the version with electrons on the right is an oxidation and its charges do not balance, and 4 e− leaves −5 on the left against −7 on the right.
x: This is balanced for an acidic solution. A basic solution has almost no H⁺, so the H⁺ must be converted with OH⁻.
Chlorine is reduced here, so electrons are gained on the reactant side. As written the charges are −1 and −13.
Check the charge: with 4 electrons the left side is −5 while the right side is −7.

q:
Acidified permanganate reacts with hydrogen peroxide as shown in the balanced equation. Which statements are true?
I. H2O2 is the oxidizing agent.
II. The oxidation state of oxygen in H2O2 changes from −1 to −2.
III. Ten electrons are transferred in the equation as written.

f.text: 2 MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(aq) + 5 H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 6 H<sup>+</sup>(aq) → 2 Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 5 O<sub>2</sub>(g) + 8 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)

h: Find where the oxygen atoms of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> end up: in O<sub>2</sub> or in H<sub>2</sub>O? Then count electrons using Mn.
w: I is false: the peroxide oxygen goes from −1 to 0 in O2, so H2O2 is oxidized and is the reducing agent; MnO4− is the oxidizing agent. II is false for the same reason: the oxygen of H2O2 becomes O2 (0); the water oxygen comes from permanganate. III is true: each Mn goes from +7 to +2, so 2 Mn gain 10 e−, matching 5 H2O2 each losing 2 e−. Answer: III only.
x: Statement I is false. H₂O₂ loses electrons as it forms O₂, so it is oxidized.
Statement II is false. The peroxide oxygen ends up in O₂, where its oxidation state is 0.
Statements I and II are both false. Check what H₂O₂ turns into.

q: In a strongly basic solution, zinc metal reduces nitrate ion to ammonia, as shown (unbalanced). When the equation is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients, how many electrons are transferred?
h: Find the change in oxidation state of N (in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub>) and of Zn, then match electrons lost and gained.
w: N goes from +5 in NO3− to −3 in NH3, gaining 8 e−; each Zn goes from 0 to +2, losing 2 e−, so 4 Zn are needed. Balanced: 4 Zn + NO3− + 7 OH− + 6 H2O → 4 Zn(OH)42− + NH3, with 8 electrons transferred (charge −8 on both sides). 2 is the loss from one Zn, 4 is the number of Zn atoms, and 16 counts the same electrons twice.
x: That is the loss from a single Zn atom. The N atom gains more than that, so more Zn is needed.
This is the number of Zn atoms in the balanced equation, not the electrons.
Electrons lost by Zn are the same electrons gained by N. Count them once.

q: The potential of a galvanic cell was measured at 25 °C for several values of the reaction quotient Q, and E is plotted against log Q. Using E = E° − (0.0592 V/n) log Q, what are E° and n for the cell reaction?
h: E° is the potential where log Q = 0. The slope of the line equals −0.0592 V/n.
w: At log Q = 0 (Q = 1) the line reads E = E° = 0.62 V. Slope = (0.541 − 0.699) V / (4 − (−4)) = −0.0198 V per unit of log Q = −0.0592/n, so n = 0.0592/0.0198 = 3.0: E° = 0.62 V; n = 3. With n = 1 the slope would be −0.0592 V, three times steeper; n = 2 gives −0.0296 V. 0.70 V is E at log Q = −4, not at standard conditions.
x: With n = 1 the line would fall 0.0592 V for each unit of log Q. Measure the slope on the graph.
E° is the potential when Q = 1, which is where log Q = 0, not at the left edge.
With n = 2 the line would drop 0.0296 V per unit of log Q. Recheck the slope.

q:
Using the standard reduction potentials in the table, rank these species in order of INCREASING strength as oxidizing agents.
I. Cu2+(aq)
II. Fe3+(aq)
III. I2(s)
h: An oxidizing agent is reduced. The more positive its reduction potential, the stronger it pulls electrons.
w: Oxidizing agents are the species on the left of the half-reactions; strength follows E°: Cu2+ (+0.34 V) < I2 (+0.54 V) < Fe3+ (+0.77 V), so I < III < II. The reversed order ranks them as reducing agents would be ranked, and I2 is not weaker than Cu2+, since its E° is higher.
x: This order is reversed. A higher reduction potential means a stronger oxidizing agent.
I₂ has a higher reduction potential than Cu²⁺, so it is the stronger oxidizing agent of the two.
Compare I₂ and Fe³⁺ again. The species with the larger E° is the stronger oxidizing agent.

q:
Using the standard reduction potentials in the table, rank these species in order of INCREASING strength as reducing agents.
I. Al(s)
II. Fe2+(aq)
III. Sn(s)
h: A reducing agent is oxidized, so look for each species on the RIGHT side of a half-reaction. The more negative that E°, the stronger the reducing agent.
w: Fe2+ acts as a reducing agent when it is oxidized to Fe3+, the reverse of the +0.77 V half-reaction (the −0.44 V row uses Fe2+ as an oxidizing agent). Sn is the product of the −0.14 V row and Al of the −1.66 V row. Lower E° means stronger reducing agent: Fe2+ (+0.77) < Sn (−0.14) < Al (−1.66), so II < III < I.
x: This order is reversed. The metal with the most negative reduction potential gives up electrons most easily.
To act as a reducing agent Fe²⁺ must be oxidized to Fe³⁺. Use the row where Fe²⁺ is the product.
Al has the most negative reduction potential of all, so it is not weaker than Sn.

q:
Using the standard reduction potentials in the table, which metals dissolve in 1 M HNO3 (nitrate is reduced to NO) but do NOT dissolve in 1 M HCl? Assume standard conditions.
I. Au
II. Cu
III. Ag
h: In HCl the only oxidizing agent is H<sup>+</sup> (0.00 V); in HNO<sub>3</sub>, nitrate (+0.96 V) is available too. A metal dissolves if the oxidant’s E° is higher.
w: I is false: Au3+/Au (+1.50 V) is above nitrate (+0.96 V), so gold dissolves in neither acid. II is true: Cu2+/Cu (+0.34 V) is above H+/H2 (0.00 V) but below nitrate, so copper dissolves only in HNO3. III is true for the same reason: Ag+/Ag (+0.80 V) lies between 0.00 and +0.96 V. Answer: II and III only.
x: Statement III is true as well. Silver’s reduction potential, +0.80 V, is still below that of nitrate.
Statement II is true as well. Copper is above H⁺ but below nitrate in the table.
Statement I is false. Gold’s reduction potential is higher than nitrate’s, so nitric acid cannot oxidize it.

q: The cell shown has a cobalt electrode (A) in 1 M Co<sup>2+</sup> and a platinum electrode (B) in a solution of 1 M Br<sup>−</sup> saturated with Br<sub>2</sub>. Using the table, what does the voltmeter read at 25 °C?
h: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), using the reduction potentials as listed. Reduction potentials are not multiplied by coefficients.
w: Br2 has the higher E°, so it is reduced at the platinum cathode (B) and cobalt is oxidized at A. E°cell = 1.07 − (−0.28) = 1.35 V. 0.79 V adds the two values without reversing the cobalt sign, 2.42 V doubles the bromine potential (E° is intensive), and 1.07 V treats the platinum half-cell as if it alone sets the voltage.
x: Subtract the anode reduction potential from the cathode one. Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Potentials are intensive and are never multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.
The cell voltage depends on both half-cells, not just the Br₂ half-cell.

q: An external power supply replaces the voltmeter in a Cu/Zn cell, as shown, and pushes electrons through the wire in the direction of the arrow (from A to B). All solutions are 1 M. Using the table, which reaction occurs, and what voltage must the supply exceed?
c: Cu(s) + Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Zn(s); more than 1.10 V
Zn(s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s); more than 1.10 V
Cu(s) + Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Zn(s); more than 0 V
Cu(s) + Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Zn(s); more than 0.42 V
h: Electrons are delivered to B, so reduction happens there. Is that the spontaneous direction for this pair of half-cells?
w: Electrons arrive at B, so Zn2+ + 2e− → Zn plates out there (cathode), and copper at A is oxidized (anode): Cu(s) + Zn2+(aq) → Cu2+(aq) + Zn(s); more than 1.10 V. This is the reverse of the spontaneous Daniell reaction, with E° = −0.76 − 0.34 = −1.10 V, so the supply must provide more than 1.10 V to drive it. The spontaneous reaction would send electrons from B to A instead. 0.42 V comes from adding the two potentials.
x: This is the spontaneous reaction, which would push electrons from the zinc to the copper. The arrow shows the opposite direction.
This reaction is nonspontaneous, so any small voltage would not be enough. The supply has to overcome the cell’s own potential.
The size of the cell potential is the difference between the two reduction potentials, not their sum.

q: Nickel is plated from a NiSO<sub>4</sub> solution at constant current. The graph shows the mass of nickel deposited on the cathode against time. What current was used? (Ni: 58.69 g mol<sup>−1</sup>; F = 96,485 C mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Read one point (mass and time). Convert mass to moles of Ni, then to moles of electrons (Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Ni), then to coulombs, and divide by seconds.
w: At 60.0 min, 2.19 g Ni = 2.19/58.69 = 0.0373 mol Ni, which needs 2 × 0.0373 = 0.0746 mol e− = 0.0746 × 96,485 = 7.20×103 C. Dividing by 3600 s gives 2.00 A. Leaving out the 2 electrons per Ni gives 1.00 A, using 4 electrons per Ni gives 4.00 A, and dividing the charge by 60.0 min instead of 3600 s gives 120 A.
x: Each Ni²⁺ ion needs two electrons to become a Ni atom. Include that factor.
Ni²⁺ gains two electrons, not four. Recheck the electron count per Ni.
An ampere is a coulomb per SECOND. Convert the minutes on the graph to seconds.

q: The cell shown has a tin electrode (A) in 1.0 M Sn<sup>2+</sup> and a lead electrode (B) in 0.0010 M Pb<sup>2+</sup>. Using the table and E = E° − (0.0592 V/n) log Q, which electrode is the anode at 25 °C, and what does the voltmeter read?
h: Write the reaction with tin as the anode and find E with the Nernst equation. A negative E means the reaction actually runs the other way.
w: For Sn + Pb2+ → Sn2+ + Pb, E° = −0.13 − (−0.14) = +0.01 V and Q = [Sn2+]/[Pb2+] = 1.0/0.0010 = 1000. E = 0.01 − (0.0592/2)(3) = -0.079 V. The negative value means the reverse reaction is spontaneous: lead is oxidized, so B is the anode; 0.079 V. The small E° is easily overturned by the 1000-fold concentration ratio. 0.010 V ignores the concentrations, 0.099 V adds the Nernst term, and 0.168 V uses n = 1.
x: This is the standard potential, but the Pb²⁺ concentration is far below 1 M. Apply the Nernst equation.
The Nernst term is subtracted when Q is greater than 1. Recheck the sign.
Both metals transfer two electrons per atom, so n is 2.

q: A standard hydrogen electrode (A: Pt in 1 M H<sup>+</sup> with H<sub>2</sub> at 1 atm) is connected to a cadmium electrode (B) in 1 M Cd<sup>2+</sup>. The meter reads 0.40 V, and electrons flow through the wire from B to A, as drawn. What is the standard reduction potential of Cd<sup>2+</sup>/Cd?
h: Electrons leave the anode. E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), and the SHE is 0.00 V by definition.
w: Electrons leave B, so cadmium is oxidized (anode) and H+ is reduced at the SHE (cathode). 0.40 V = 0.00 V − E°(Cd2+/Cd), so E° = −0.40 V. A positive value would make Cd2+ easier to reduce than H+, which would send electrons the other way. E° is not divided by the 2 electrons.
x: If Cd²⁺ had a positive reduction potential, the SHE would be the anode and electrons would flow from A to B.
Electrode potentials are not divided by the number of electrons transferred.
The SHE contributes 0.00 V, so the meter reading alone sets the size of the cadmium potential.

q:
Aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolyzed between inert platinum electrodes. Which statements are true?
I. O2 gas forms at the anode.
II. Sodium metal is deposited at the cathode.
III. The solution near the cathode becomes acidic.
h: At the cathode, compare how hard it is to reduce Na<sup>+</sup> and water. Sulfate is very hard to oxidize, so think about what water does at the anode.
w: I is true: sulfate resists oxidation, so water is oxidized at the anode, 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H+ + 4e−. II is false: water (−0.83 V) is far easier to reduce than Na+ (−2.71 V), so H2 forms instead of sodium. III is false: reducing water makes OH−, so the solution near the cathode becomes basic (the anode region becomes acidic). Answer: I only.
x: Statement II is false. Water is reduced far more easily than Na⁺ in aqueous solution.
Statement III is false. Reducing water releases OH⁻ ions at the cathode.
Statements II and III are both false. Look at the cathode products in the table.

q: An alkaline dry cell runs on the overall reaction shown, in a basic KOH paste. Which half-reaction occurs at the cathode?
h: The cathode is where reduction happens. Find the element whose oxidation state drops, and remember the electrolyte is basic.
w: Mn goes from +4 in MnO2 to +3 in MnO(OH), a reduction, so it happens at the cathode. Balanced for a basic medium: MnO2 + H2O + e− → MnO(OH) + OH− (H, O and charge balance). The zinc half-reaction is the oxidation at the anode; the H+ version suits an acid, not a KOH paste; the remaining manganese choice runs the change backward, as an oxidation.
x: Zinc loses electrons here, which is oxidation. That happens at the anode.
This balances atoms with H⁺, but the electrolyte is basic, so water and OH⁻ are used instead.
This releases electrons, so it is an oxidation. In the battery, manganese is reduced.

q: Permanganate oxidizes chloride ion in acidic solution, as shown in the balanced equation. Using the table, what is ΔG° for the reaction as written at 25 °C? (F = 96,485 C mol<sup>−1</sup>)

f.text: 2 MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(aq) + 10 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) + 16 H<sup>+</sup>(aq) → 2 Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 5 Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) + 8 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)

h: Find E° first, then count the electrons transferred in the equation as written: n is the total, not the number in one half-reaction.
w: E° = 1.507 − 1.358 = 0.149 V. In the equation as written, 2 Mn each gain 5 e− (and 10 Cl− each lose 1), so n = 10. ΔG° = −nFE° = −(10)(96,485)(0.149) J = -143.8 kJ ≈ −144 kJ. n = 1 gives −14.4 kJ and n = 2 (one Cl2) gives −28.8 kJ; a positive E° always gives a negative ΔG°.
x: n must be the total number of electrons transferred in the full equation as written.
Two electrons form one Cl₂, but the equation makes five Cl₂. Count all the electrons.
A positive cell potential means a negative ΔG°. Check the sign.

q: In the galvanic cell shown, metal X (electrode A) dips into 1 M X<sup>2+</sup> and metal Y (electrode B) into 1 M Y<sup>2+</sup>. The labels on the salt bridge show the direction the ions move while the cell runs. Which statement must be true?
c: X is oxidized; E° of X<sup>2+</sup>/X is lower than E° of Y<sup>2+</sup>/Y
Y is oxidized; E° of Y<sup>2+</sup>/Y is lower than E° of X<sup>2+</sup>/X
X is reduced; E° of X<sup>2+</sup>/X is higher than E° of Y<sup>2+</sup>/Y
X is oxidized; E° of X<sup>2+</sup>/X is higher than E° of Y<sup>2+</sup>/Y
h: Cations in the salt bridge move toward the cathode, where positive ions are being used up. Anions move toward the anode.
w: Cations move toward B and anions toward A, so B is the cathode (Y2+ is reduced there, removing positive charge) and A is the anode, where X is oxidized and X2+ builds up. In a spontaneous cell the anode couple has the lower reduction potential: X is oxidized; E° of X2+/X is lower than E° of Y2+/Y. Reading the ion arrows backward would make Y the anode.
x: Anions move toward the anode to balance the positive ions made there. In the drawing anions move toward A.
Cations move toward the cathode. In the drawing they move toward B, so reduction is not at A.
The anode is right, but in a spontaneous cell the metal that is oxidized has the lower reduction potential.

q: The tetrahedral ion [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is blue and high spin. Which crystal-field diagram correctly shows the d electrons of cobalt in this ion?
h: Find the oxidation state of Co and its d-electron count. In a tetrahedral field the splitting is the reverse of octahedral: two orbitals (e) lie lower and three (t<sub>2</sub>) higher.
w: With four Cl− and a 2− charge, cobalt is Co2+, a d7 ion. A tetrahedral field puts the e set below the t2 set, and its small splitting makes the complex high spin: e4t23, with 3 unpaired electrons, which is diagram I. II uses the octahedral ordering (three orbitals lower), III pairs electrons in t2 while an orbital is empty (low spin, which tetrahedral complexes essentially never are), and IV holds only six electrons.
x: This places the three orbitals below the two. That is the octahedral pattern, not the tetrahedral one.
A high-spin ion fills each orbital singly before pairing. This diagram pairs electrons while a t₂ orbital is empty.
Count the electrons. Co²⁺ has seven d electrons, and this diagram shows six.

q: The crystal-field diagram shows the d electrons of the metal ion in an octahedral complex. Which complex does it represent?
h: Count the electrons drawn and check whether any are paired while e<sub>g</sub> is still empty. That gives the d count and the field strength.
w: The diagram holds four electrons, all in t2g with one pair: a low-spin d4 ion with 2 unpaired electrons. Mn3+ is d4, and CN− is a strong-field ligand that favors pairing, so [Mn(CN)6]3− fits. [Mn(H2O)6]3+ is d4 but high spin (t2g3eg1, 4 unpaired); Cr3+ is d3; Fe2+ is d6.
x: Water is a weak-field ligand, so the fourth electron would go singly into the upper level rather than pair. Count the unpaired electrons drawn.
Cr³⁺ has only three d electrons, and the diagram shows four.
Fe²⁺ has six d electrons. A low-spin d⁶ ion would fill all three lower orbitals with pairs.

q: The graph shows the visible absorption spectra of two octahedral cobalt(III) complexes, X and Y, that differ only in their ligands. Which complex has the larger crystal-field splitting Δ<sub>o</sub>, and what is that Δ<sub>o</sub>? (h = 6.626×10<sup>−34</sup> J s; c = 2.998×10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>; N<sub>A</sub> = 6.022×10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Δ<sub>o</sub> equals the energy of the light absorbed. Shorter wavelength means higher energy: E = hc/λ per ion, times N<sub>A</sub> per mole.
w: X absorbs at the shorter wavelength (470 nm), so its photons carry more energy and X has the larger Δo. Δo = hcNA/λ = (6.626×10−34)(2.998×108)(6.022×1023)/(470×10−9 m) = 254522 J mol−1, so X; 255 kJ mol−1. 203 kJ mol−1 is the value for Y’s 590 nm peak, the smaller splitting.
x: Y absorbs at the longer wavelength, which is the lower energy, so its splitting is the smaller one.
The complex is right, but 203 kJ/mol comes from the 590 nm peak. Use the wavelength X absorbs.
The energy is right for X’s peak, but the complex that absorbs there is not Y.
